# Draftera

> Draftera is the AI operations practice of Ken Hopkins, a former nonprofit executive director. It helps Canadian nonprofits and social enterprises put AI to work on routine tasks, with clear rules and staff in charge of every decision. Its services are built on Draftera Foundations, a framework for using AI in nonprofits and social enterprises. Based in Newfoundland and Labrador, working with nonprofits across Canada.

Draftera works with nonprofits, charities, social enterprises and associations, typically with annual revenue between about $1 million and $20 million, and with the networks, associations and funders that support them. It offers three fixed-price ways to start. Prices are in Canadian dollars, plus applicable taxes. Any new AI tool licences are paid directly by the client organization. Every engagement starts with a free 30-minute conversation and, if working together makes sense, a written proposal with a fixed price before any work begins.

## Three ways to start

- [AI policy and staff session](https://draftera.ca/services.html#ai-policy-staff-session) $1,950. For an organization whose staff already use AI tools without shared rules, or whose board is asking about AI. A board-approved AI policy, a one-page guide for staff, plain rules on what information stays out of AI tools, wording for the board minutes, one round of revisions and a 90-minute session for staff. It takes about three weeks from the first call to the staff session. A board and leadership session, a full data and privacy review (practical guidance, not legal advice) and a public transparency statement are available on request.
- [Group workshop](https://draftera.ca/services.html#group-workshop) $1,500, or $2,500 for a half day. For networks, associations and funders who want to help several organizations at once. A planning call, a 90-minute session for up to 25 people (online or in person), a handout and a checklist each organization can use to see where it stands. The half-day version adds time for each organization to start its own policy.
- [Workflow Build](https://draftera.ca/workflow-build.html) $2,500 for one workflow, $4,000 for two. For an organization with a recurring task that takes too much staff time, such as funder reports, intake records, meeting follow-up or donor thank-you letters. One working workflow built with staff over two to three weeks on the tools the organization already has where possible, staff training, a short written guide to what is permitted and who checks the output, and a final report.

## Ongoing support

- [Draftera Embedded AI Partnership](https://draftera.ca/partnership.html) Monthly support for organizations that have seen a workflow work and want more, about two days a month on Core and about four on Plus. It covers new workflows, staff training, maintenance, operational support (process simplification, change management, and role and structure reviews), reporting and a yearly Foundations Check-up. Core is $2,500 a month for one active priority at a time, and Plus is $4,500 a month for up to two active priorities at once. Both have a three-month minimum and then run month to month, and an organization can switch between them with 30 days' notice.

## The framework

- [Draftera Foundations](https://draftera.ca/foundations.html) The method behind every Draftera service, reviewed annually. It sets out six pieces an organization needs in place to use AI safely, openly and to real benefit. Four concern governing AI (leadership and policy, data and privacy, human oversight, and transparency and trust) and two concern using it (people and skills, and value and measurement). An inventory and annual review keeps every piece current, and the full framework can be built in stages. It draws on the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the OECD AI Principles and Canadian standards and guidance, including CAN/DGSI 101, the National Standard of Canada for the ethical design and use of AI by small and medium organizations. Draftera prepares organizations for independent verification against CAN/DGSI 101, which is optional and carried out by the Digital Governance Council for its own fee. Draftera does not certify organizations and is independent of the Council. The framework is practical guidance, not legal advice.

## For partners

- [For partners](https://draftera.ca/partners.html) For networks, associations and funders, the first step is usually a group workshop. A policy template or AI module for member resource libraries, group delivery of the framework for a cohort, an aggregate summary of where grantees stand on AI governance, and guidance for grantees on disclosing AI use can follow. Work beyond the workshop is scoped to fit.

## How the work is done

- Client, donor and staff personal information never goes into outside AI tools without the organization's written agreement.
- Every workflow has a named person who checks what it produces, and staff remain responsible for the work.
- Draftera is tool-neutral and builds on tools the organization already has wherever possible, such as Microsoft 365, Google Workspace or an existing AI subscription.
- Results are reported plainly, including when a workflow falls short.

## About Ken Hopkins

- [About Ken](https://draftera.ca/about.html) Ken Hopkins has more than two decades of experience leading organizations through growth and change. He spent seven years (2012 to 2019) as Executive Director of the School Lunch Association in Newfoundland and Labrador, where revenue tripled and the program expanded to 34 school locations, serving over 1 million meals a year with a team of over 80 people. He also brings operational leadership experience from a large Canadian university, and for more than two years he has been building practical AI workflows with privacy safeguards, clear responsibilities and human review. He developed Draftera Foundations. He holds an MBA (Employee Relations) from the University of Leicester, a Master's Certificate in Project Management and a Certificate in Not-for-Profit Governance from Rotman, and is a Qualified Mediator.
